findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled when the request returns
findings.body: The goroutines for Create (line 51), Update (135), Delete (110) and DeleteCollection (163) build their timeout context from the incoming request `ctx`. The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which is right after the goroutine is launched. The legacy write will therefore often fail with `context canceled`, or never really run, so the 'safety' write to legacy is unreliable. Derive the context with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before adding the timeout.

findings.title: Legacy write errors in the goroutines are silently dropped
findings.body: In every async goroutine the legacy error is only turned into a boolean metric label and is never logged. When a legacy write fails, nothing records which object, name or kind failed, so it is impossible to diagnose or reconcile the divergence between the two stores. Log the error together with the object identity.

findings.title: Storage failure recorded as legacy duration in Create and Update
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails (line 45), and likewise `d.Storage.Update` (line 129), the code calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the call that failed was to unified storage. The result is wrong metrics: phantom legacy errors and missing storage errors. Use `recordStorageDuration` here.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage duration
findings.body: The async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls `recordStorageDuration` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy latencies and errors are therefore counted under the storage metric, which skews both series.

findings.title: Delete success metric uses object name as kind label
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object name where the kind is expected. This puts the wrong value in the kind label and creates an unbounded set of metric label values (cardinality explosion). It should pass `options.Kind`.

findings.title: Delete attaches the base logger to the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` drops the name, kind and method values built into `log` on the previous line. Downstream logging in Delete therefore lacks that context, unlike the other methods, which pass `log`.

findings.title: Legacy update re-applies objInfo against legacy state instead of using the storage result
findings.body: The old code wrapped the object returned by storage in `updateWrapper` before calling legacy. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `Legacy.Update`, so `UpdatedObject` is evaluated against whatever legacy currently holds. That legacy state may be stale or missing, especially for patches, and the stores can diverge. Running this concurrently after the request also lets the patch/transform functions be reused outside the request lifetime.

findings.title: Input object shared with background goroutine (data race)
findings.body: The goroutine passes `obj` to `Legacy.Create` while the handler goes on to serialize and return `created`. Storage implementations may mutate `obj` in place or return the same pointer, so legacy conversion and response encoding can touch the same object concurrently. Pass a deep copy (`obj.DeepCopyObject()`) to the async write.

findings.title: Unit tests don't verify or synchronize the async legacy writes
findings.body: Legacy and storage share one mock, and the tests never wait for or assert the legacy goroutine calls. Nothing checks that legacy is actually written, and goroutines may still call into the mock after the subtest finishes, which can cause flaky failures. Some cases also configure legacy expectations that never matter, such as the Create error case.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration tests may be flaky due to async legacy writes
findings.body: `doPlaylistTests` compares the legacy API with the k8s API immediately after k8s writes (create, then legacy list; update, then `getFromBothAPIs`). In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so if the legacy endpoints read from legacy storage these assertions race with the background write.

findings.title: Duplicate go.work.sum entry and unrelated dependency churn
findings.body: This diff adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, which already appears a few lines above. It also adds several unrelated otel/alertmanager sums. This looks like accidental tooling churn that doesn't belong in this PR.
